introduction-the-expensive-problem-with-.core: Enterprises historically linked branches with MPLS circuits from carriers: private, with QoS and SLAs, but expensive per Mbps, slow to provision (months) and hub-and-spoke, backhauling internet and SaaS traffic through headquarters. As apps moved to SaaS and cloud, sending Microsoft 365 traffic through HQ's firewall added latency and cost. SD-WAN and SASE grew out of that mismatch.

first_principles.problem: A retailer pays $1,500/month per store for 20 Mbps MPLS, and Office 365 is slow because it's backhauled to HQ.

analogy.title: Routing all mail through head office
analogy.story: Every letter from every branch goes to HQ first, even if it's addressed next door.
analogy.breaks: Mail delays are tolerated; video calls aren't.

check.q: Why did backhauling SaaS traffic through HQ become a problem?
check.a: Traffic to cloud apps travels a long detour through HQ, adding latency and consuming expensive MPLS/HQ bandwidth.

sd-wan-software-defined-wan.core: SD-WAN puts an appliance (physical or virtual) at each site that builds encrypted overlay tunnels over any transport (MPLS, broadband, LTE/5G). A central controller sets policy. Edges continuously measure each path's latency, jitter and loss, and steer each application to the best path by policy (voice on the lowest jitter, backups on the cheapest), with local internet breakout for trusted SaaS and zero-touch provisioning.

first_principles.problem: A branch has broadband and LTE, and voice quality suffers whenever broadband gets congested.
truths: Multiple links are cheaper than one premium link.

analogy.title: A satnav choosing roads per vehicle
analogy.story: Ambulances get the fastest route, trucks the cheapest; routes change live with traffic.
analogy.breaks: Satnavs plan once per trip; SD-WAN re-steers per flow continuously.

steps.label: Effect
steps.detail: Voice moves to LTE when broadband jitter rises.

code.text:
app_policies:
  - app: voip
    sla: { latency_ms: 150, jitter_ms: 30, loss_pct: 1 }
    preferred: [broadband, lte]
  - app: office365
    action: local_breakout
  - app: backup
    preferred: [broadband]
    avoid: [lte]

check.q: How does SD-WAN decide which link to use for voice traffic?
check.a: It continuously measures each path's latency, jitter and loss and sends voice over the path meeting its SLA policy.

mpls-vs-internet-overlay-making-best-eff.core: Internet links are best-effort with no SLA, but SD-WAN makes them good enough. Bonding multiple diverse links, per-packet steering, forward error correction that adds parity packets to recover loss without retransmission, packet duplication for critical flows, jitter buffers and fast failover in sub-seconds together often beat a single MPLS circuit for availability. Many enterprises keep a small MPLS link only for the most sensitive traffic.

first_principles.problem: Leadership fears replacing MPLS with 'unreliable' internet links will hurt critical apps.

analogy.title: Sending important documents by two couriers
analogy.story: If one is late, the other arrives; together they beat one premium courier's guarantee.
analogy.breaks: Couriers cost per parcel; duplication doubles bandwidth.

steps.label: Effect
steps.detail: Dual internet beats single MPLS on paper.

check.q: What does forward error correction do in SD-WAN?
check.a: Sends parity packets so lost packets can be reconstructed at the receiver without waiting for retransmission.

sase-secure-access-service-edge.core: SD-WAN fixes connectivity, but local breakout bypasses HQ's firewall. SASE (Gartner, 2019) converges networking and security into a cloud service delivered from global PoPs: SD-WAN, secure web gateway, CASB, zero-trust network access and firewall-as-a-service. Every user and site connects to the nearest PoP, and one policy engine applies regardless of location.

first_principles.problem: After enabling local internet breakout, branches lose the security inspection HQ's firewall used to provide.
truths: Users are everywhere, not in offices.
Cloud PoPs are close to users.
derivation: Connect sites and users to **nearest PoP**.

analogy.title: Airport security at every local airport
analogy.story: Instead of flying everyone to one central checkpoint, every nearby airport runs the same security standard.
analogy.breaks: Airports are physical; PoP reach depends on vendor footprint.

example.title: Branch flow
flow: Branch SD-WAN tunnels to nearest PoP
SWG inspects web, CASB checks SaaS

check.q: What's the difference between SSE and SASE?
check.a: SSE is the security services (SWG, CASB, ZTNA, FWaaS); SASE is SSE plus SD-WAN networking converged.

zero-trust-model-in-sase.core: Zero trust drops the idea that the internal network is trusted. Every request is authenticated and authorised on identity, device posture and context, and access is granted per application, not to whole networks. In SASE, ZTNA brokers connections from users to specific private apps through the PoP; the apps make outbound-only connections so they're never exposed, and policies adapt continuously, unlike flat VPN access.

first_principles.problem: A contractor's VPN account gives access to the entire corporate network, and malware on their laptop spreads laterally.

analogy.title: Hotel keycards per room vs a master key
analogy.story: Each guest's card opens only their room and the gym, and is checked at every door.
analogy.breaks: Keycards don't check health; ZTNA checks device posture too.

steps.label: Effect
steps.detail: Contractor reaches only approved apps from compliant devices.

code.text:
- app: jira.internal
  allow:
    groups: [engineering]
    device: { managed: true, disk_encrypted: true, os_min: "14.0" }
    mfa: required
- app: payroll.internal
  allow:
    groups: [hr]
    device: { managed: true }
    location_risk: low

check.q: How does ZTNA reduce lateral movement compared to VPN?
check.a: Users get access only to specific applications, not the whole network, so a compromised device can't scan or reach other systems.
